title: Measuring Validator‑Guided Repair on a Shared Initial LLM Candidate for Network Configurations
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired, validator‑grounded study (PREREG‑CAND‑001‑VER‑GVR‑2026‑09‑01) to evaluate whether a generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline changes the executability of LLM‑produced network configurations when the same single sampled candidate per intent is reused across arms (shared_initial_candidate semantics). Design and execution (N=200 paired intents; completed_episode_count=400; model_calls_used=200) used gpt‑5‑mini (declared) to produce exactly one initial generation per intent which was deterministically reused for both baseline and guarded episodes; a deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) scored validity and the guarded arm permitted one automated repair if the validator flagged violations. Results: baseline_success_count = 200/200 (100%), guarded_success_count = 200/200 (100%); paired contingency n11=200, n10=0, n01=0, n00=0; paired difference = 0.0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; paired bootstrap (seed=1729, resamples=10000) 95% percentile CI = [0.0, 0.0]. No repairs were applied because every shared initial candidate was validator‑valid. Important clarifications are (1) because shared_initial_candidate semantics were executed, the estimand measures only the downstream validator/repair effect on a fixed sampled candidate and does not measure any effect that would arise from independent per‑condition sampling, different prompts, or sampling nondeterminism; (2) the archived model configuration records temperature = null (unset), and null/unset is not evidence of deterministic sampling and does not imply temperature = 0. We report full preregistration, execution accounting, representative validator traces, and a calibrated interpretation of the null paired effect together with limitations and recommended follow‑on designs.

sections.introduction: Motivation and question. Large language models (LLMs) are being explored to translate natural‑language NetOps intents into device configuration sequences. Hallucination and unsafe outputs present operational risks, motivating verifier‑assisted pipelines that detect and (optionally) repair unsafe outputs before execution. We asked the narrow, preregistered research question: when one sampled LLM candidate per intent is deterministically reused across baseline and guarded arms (shared_initial_candidate semantics), does applying a deterministic validator plus a single automated repair attempt change the rate of validator‑valid, executable configurations relative to reusing the same candidate without validation/repair? Rationale and estimand. The paired shared‑initial design isolates downstream validator/repair effects on a fixed initial candidate (primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline). This design does not measure effects due to independent per‑condition sampling, alternative prompting, or sampling nondeterminism; those are outside the executed estimand by design and must not be conflated with the present results. Contributions. (1) A fully preregistered, artifacted paired confirmatory experiment and deterministic scoring pipeline; (2) a validator‑grounded analysis on 200 paired intents using gpt‑5‑mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5; (3) transparent reporting and interpretation of a null paired effect arising from shared_initial_candidate execution semantics, with concrete recommendations for follow‑on confirmatory designs.
sections.related_work: Context. Surveys and empirical studies document hallucination and reliability issues for LLMs across domains and motivate evidence‑grounded generation and verification [1,2]. Retrieval‑ and evidence‑grounded designs can reduce hallucination in operations‑style QA tasks [2]. Tool‑assisted generate–validate–repair architectures have been proposed and shown to improve correctness in infrastructure‑as‑code and related code‑generation tasks (e.g., TerraFormer) though demonstrations are typically outside device‑level NetOps execution studies [3]. Prior NetOps LLM evaluations have measured translation capability but, in the supplied literature, do not provide standardized execution‑level safety measurements in packet‑level simulators [4]. This gap motivated our preregistered confirmatory run, designed specifically to produce machine‑verifiable execution artifacts and deterministic validator traces.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and design. The experiment was preregistered as PREREG‑CAND‑001‑VER‑GVR‑2026‑09‑01 with a paired confirmatory design (task_count = 200 paired intents). Sampling and tasks. A deterministic task bank of 200 synthetic 'intent_configuration_repair_v1' intents was selected before any model calls. Generation semantics and model. Execution used shared_initial_candidate semantics: exactly one initial generation per intent was produced and deterministically reused for both baseline and guarded episodes. Declared model: gpt‑5‑mini via the hosted adapter 'openai_responses' (execution accounting: model_calls_used = 200; execution manifest completed_episode_count = 400). The archived model configuration file is execution/model_configuration.json (sha256: a40e96e212ab87da251ac0d6dbb75bc543afa13438b5a6b9ebd073597ffdd820); that file records temperature = null (unset). Explicit note: temperature = null/unset is not evidence of deterministic sampling and does not imply temperature = 0. Validator and repair. We used deterministic_netops_validator_v5 to convert candidate configurations to a binary valid/invalid executable label (scoring_rule = full_intent_constraint_validation). For guarded episodes a single automated repair attempt was permitted if the validator detected violations. Generation and execution semantics. Under shared_initial_candidate semantics baseline and guarded reused the exact same candidate; no independent first‑pass draws per condition were executed. This means any observed difference between arms can only arise from deterministic validation or the permitted repair applied to that same candidate. Scoring and analysis. Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. Primary test: exact two‑sided McNemar on the paired 2×2 table; we report exact p‑values and absolute risk difference with 95% paired bootstrap percentile CIs (bootstrap_seed=1729, bootstrap_resamples=10000). Analysis followed the preregistered complete_pair_primary policy and sensitivity plans. Reproducibility. All inputs, provider traces, validator traces, and analysis artifacts were recorded; representative artifact paths and hashes are available in the archived evidence bundle.
sections.results: Execution accounting. The adapter completed the preregistered run: planned_episode_count = 400, completed_episode_count = 400, failed_episode_count = 0, model_calls_used = 200. Scoring outcomes. Baseline_success_count = 200/200 (100%), guarded_success_count = 200/200 (100%). Paired contingency: n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0; paired difference = 0.0. Exact McNemar two‑sided test: p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap (seed = 1729; 10,000 resamples) 95% percentile CI = [0.0, 0.0]. Repair activity. Because every shared initial candidate was validator‑valid, no repair prompts were issued and no repairs were applied in guarded episodes; validator traces for representative tasks (e.g., task‑000004, task‑000005) are included in the archived artifacts and show validator.valid = true and validator.final_configuration matching the shared candidate. Interpretation of inferential metrics. The McNemar test and reported p = 1.0 in this dataset reflect a degenerate case with zero discordant pairs (n10 = n01 = 0); under that degeneracy the test is uninformative about potential repair efficacy under alternative sampling regimes. The bootstrap CI [0.0,0.0] similarly reflects the observed absence of any paired difference in this executed estimand. Contamination and missingness. All preregistered contamination checks and missingness summaries passed; no pairs were excluded and no episodes were failed or unscorable.
sections.discussion: Why a null paired effect arose. The null effect directly follows from the executed design: a single sampled candidate per intent (shared_initial_candidate) was valid under the deterministic validator for all 200 tasks; therefore the permitted repair could not alter any outcome. Scientific meaning and limits. The run demonstrates a complete, machine‑verifiable GVR evaluation pipeline with deterministic scoring and transparent artifact capture. Crucially, it does not demonstrate that (a) GVR would be unnecessary under independent per‑condition sampling, (b) other models or prompts would produce similarly valid candidates, or (c) repairs would not help under adversarial or more challenging task subsets. Threats to validity. Internal: shared_initial_candidate semantics restrict internal validity to downstream validator/repair effects on a fixed candidate; archived model_configuration.json records temperature = null (unset), which is not evidence of deterministic sampling. Construct: synthetic intents and an abstracted deterministic validator may omit vendor CLI idiosyncrasies and dynamic device interactions. External: single model/provider and absence of live hardware/emulation limit generalizability. Practical recommendations. To test repair efficacy under realistic sampling variability, future confirmatory runs should (1) use independent per‑condition first‑pass sampling (produce separate baseline and guarded draws), (2) include adversarial/challenging task subsets to increase expected discordant pairs, (3) expand model diversity and controlled temperature settings, and (4) increase validator fidelity to vendor‑specific behaviors or use packet‑level emulation to capture runtime effects. These concrete design changes change the estimand from downstream validator/repair effect on a fixed candidate to the end‑to‑end effect of guarded generation plus validation under sampling variability.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory experiment to measure whether applying a deterministic validator and a single automated repair to a fixed LLM‑generated candidate changes executable correctness. Under shared_initial_candidate semantics with gpt‑5‑mini (N=200 paired intents) every sampled candidate was validator‑valid and no repairs were applied; therefore the guarded pipeline produced no measurable improvement relative to baseline (paired difference = 0.0, McNemar p = 1.0, bootstrap CI [0.0,0.0]). The study establishes a reproducible artifacted evaluation workflow and emphasizes that experimental semantics (shared_initial_candidate; temperature=null recorded) crucially constrain interpretation. Follow‑on preregistered designs that execute independent per‑condition sampling, adversarial tasks, and broader model/validator diversity are required to evaluate repair efficacy under realistic sampling variability.

disclosure_statement: Disclosure (concise): The human Research Director selected the broad topic family (Generative AI / LLMs for NetOps) prior to the autonomy lock. After the lock the autonomous system performed literature review, experiment selection, preregistration (PREREG‑CAND‑001‑VER‑GVR‑2026‑09‑01), code generation, execution, analysis, and manuscript drafting without manual human editing of technical content. Declared model: gpt‑5‑mini via hosted adapter 'openai_responses' (execution used model_calls_used = 200; execution/model_configuration.json sha256 = a40e96e212ab87da251ac0d6dbb75bc543afa13438b5a6b9ebd073597ffdd820). Generation semantics executed: shared_initial_candidate — exactly one sampled initial generation per intent was produced and deterministically reused for both baseline and guarded conditions (no independent per‑condition first‑pass sampling). The archived model_configuration.json records temperature = null (unset); null/unset is not evidence of deterministic sampling and does not imply temperature = 0. Validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 scored candidates and a single automated repair iteration was permitted in guarded episodes; in this run the validator flagged no violations and no repairs were applied. Execution accounting: completed_episode_count = 400 (200 paired intents), completed without preregistration deviations (execution manifest preregistration_sha256 = f0c8330d3d74cb95461d3f0291ba1b607c427ad37b5edc3750cad593bd4aae76). Master prompt immutable reference: provenance/master_prompt.txt — 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba. Pre‑lock infrastructure development and rehearsal occurred but pre‑lock artifacts were not used as empirical evidence in this final run. After the autonomy lock no human manually rewrote technical results, manuscript text, figures, or references.
limitations: Shared_initial_candidate semantics: a single sampled initial generation was reused across baseline and guarded conditions; this design measures validator/repair effects only and cannot detect differences caused by independent per‑condition sampling or prompt engineering.

Temperature unset (temperature=null) in the archived model_configuration.json: null/unset is not evidence of deterministic sampling and does not imply temperature=0; sampling nondeterminism may still have occurred during the single sampled generation.
Single model and single hosted provider: results reflect gpt‑5‑mini under the archived adapter; generalization to other models or model families is unsupported by these artifacts.

Synthetic task bank and validator abstraction: tasks were synthetic 'intent_configuration_repair_v1' items and the deterministic validator is an abstraction; realistic vendor CLI idiosyncrasies, emergent runtime interactions, and hardware effects were not executed on live devices.

No observed validator failures: all initial candidates were validator‑valid, so the experiment could not assess the repair step's effectiveness; the null effect therefore reflects the task/sampling conditions rather than evidence that GVR is unnecessary in general.
